questions.q: A sign of a cold solder joint:
options: A thin, even layer of solder over the pad
questions.explain: The solder didn't wet one of the sides; the joint breaks from vibration.

questions.q: Why tin both the wire and the pad before joining?
options: So that both sides get wetted
To avoid overheating the board and pad
questions.explain: Tinned surfaces join in 1–2 s without overheating.

questions.q: Where do you secure a wire with a zip tie?
options: Right against the joint for rigidity
questions.explain: A rigid point right next to another rigid point breaks the strands at the boundary.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you strip insulation with a knife?
options: The knife gets dull on the copper strands
questions.explain: A gauge-matched stripper doesn't damage the strands.

questions.q: Which flux is unacceptable on electronics?
questions.explain: Active flux eats away traces and wires.

questions.q: How do you check a power solder joint under load?
options: A multimeter continuity test for an open
questions.explain: A bad connection heats up under current (without props): a thermal camera or, carefully, a finger.

questions.q: Tip temperature for Sn63/Pb37 leaded solder:
questions.explain: The solder melts at 183 °C; the tip is kept at 330–370 °C to heat the joint quickly.

questions.q: Why isn't the tinned section of a wire made longer than the pad?
options: Otherwise the wire conducts current worse
It becomes stiff and breaks at the edge
questions.explain: The extra tinned section loses flexibility; the wire breaks at the boundary with the flexible part.
